variants.mt_reading: the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive
variants.variant_reading: sons of God — the MT reads bene ha-elohim here. The question at this verse is interpretive: divine beings, or humans (the line of Seth, or rulers). Interpretive evidence, not a witness to the text: 1 Enoch 6–16 (the Book of the Watchers, non-canonical, 4th–3rd c. BC) retells the episode with angels, the Watchers, as the sons of God.
variants.variant_original: Same text in the MT and the critical LXX; some Greek manuscripts differ (see the LXX_manuscript_variant case)
variants.heiser_analysis: Heiser argues that every OT usage of bene ha-elohim / bene elohim refers to divine beings, never to human lineages. The phrase is used in Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7 unambiguously of divine beings presenting before Yahweh. He regards the human readings as later innovations to avoid the 'offensive' reading of divine-human interbreeding: the rabbinic 'sons of the great ones' or judges, and the Christian Sethite view (Julius Africanus, Augustine). In his view the Watchers tradition (1 Enoch 6-16, non-canonical) preserves the older, correct understanding that the sons of God in Genesis 6 were divine beings who transgressed their proper domain.
variants.scholarly_consensus: Heiser and other divine-council scholars hold that bene ha-elohim here means divine beings: the reading of the earliest extant Jewish interpreters and, as they read them, of Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4. Others read the phrase of humans: the godly line of Seth (Julius Africanus and Augustine; later Calvin, and Keil and Delitzsch) or, in rabbinic tradition, rulers or judges (Targum Onkelos: 'sons of the great ones').
variants.preferred_for_hlt: the sons of God (divine beings) saw that the daughters of Adam were beautiful
variants.hlt_rationale: The Hebrew bene ha-elohim always refers to divine beings in the OT (Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7). The Sethite interpretation is rejected as a later theological alteration of meaning. The HLT makes the divine nature of these beings explicit.

variants.mt_reading: the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive
variants.variant_reading: the angels of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful
variants.scholarly_consensus: The critical LXX text (Rahlfs) agrees with the MT: ἰδόντες δὲ οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τὰς θυγατέρας τῶν ἀνθρώπων. The manuscript reading οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ is generally taken as an interpretive change within the Greek tradition rather than evidence for a different Hebrew text. Philo (Gig. 6, quoting this verse; Deus 1, on 6:4) and Josephus (Antiquities 1.73: πολλοὶ γὰρ ἄγγελοι θεοῦ γυναιξὶ συνιόντες, 'many angels of God accompanied with women', Whiston) also speak of 'angels of God': non-canonical evidence of how the verse was read in the first century, not witnesses to its text.

witnesses.manuscript: LXX, critical text (Rahlfs: οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ)
Some LXX manuscripts, including Codex Alexandrinus (first hand)

variants.mt_reading: Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven
variants.mt_hebrew: וַיהוָה הִמְטִיר עַל־סְדֹם וְעַל־עֲמֹרָה גָּפְרִית וָאֵשׁ מֵאֵת יְהוָה מִן־הַשָּׁמָיִם
variants.variant_reading: The MT preserves the remarkable two-Yahweh reading: one Yahweh on the ground (who has been present with Abraham in human form since Genesis 18:1) rains fire from another Yahweh in heaven. This is a key two-powers-in-heaven text.
variants.heiser_analysis: Heiser identifies this as one of the clearest two-powers-in-heaven texts. The visible Yahweh (who appeared to Abraham at Mamre in human form, ate food, and walked with Abraham) rains fire from the invisible Yahweh in heaven. The text deliberately uses the name Yahweh twice — not 'the LORD rained fire from heaven' but 'Yahweh rained fire from Yahweh out of heaven.' This is the second Yahweh figure — the pre-incarnate Christ.
variants.scholarly_consensus: The double use of Yahweh is preserved in all major textual traditions. Alan Segal identified this as a key 'two powers' text in Jewish theology.
variants.preferred_for_hlt: Then Yahweh (the visible Yahweh on earth, Jesus) rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh (the invisible Yahweh) out of heaven
variants.hlt_rationale: The MT preserves the two-Yahweh reading. The HLT makes explicit what the text clearly states: two distinct Yahweh figures acting in concert — one visible on earth, one in heaven.
